title: Flow Matching Alignment for Few-Shot Learning
one_liner: Instead of adjusting features once, take many small steps to gradually align image features to text features using a learned velocity field.
lead: When a pre-trained vision-language model like CLIP sees a new task with only a few example images, it struggles because image and text features are far apart in their shared space. Today's methods adjust features in one pass, which fails on difficult classes where the gap is wide. This paper proposes FMA: learn a velocity field (a rule for which direction to nudge features at each moment) so that image features can drift toward text features gradually over many steps, like a guided walk instead of one big jump.

problem.h2: One-step adjustment fails on distant features
paras: A pre-trained vision-language model has an image encoder and a text encoder. Both produce lists of numbers (called features) that should point to the same thing when trained well. For everyday classes in the training data, they are already pretty close. But for rare classes with only a few examples, the image features and text features sit far apart in the space of possible numbers.

Today's parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods — prompt tuning, LoRA, adapters — all make one adjustment pass: tweak the model weights once, and in one forward step through the model, image features nudge toward text features. When the gap is small, this works. When the gap is large and the class is difficult (features are highly tangled with other classes), one nudge is not enough.

callout.html: One-step adjustments cannot handle complex transformations where image and text features need to travel a long distance through feature space.

steps.text: Use CLIP encoders to turn images into lists of numbers and class names into lists of numbers.
For each class, match each image feature to its correct text feature (not random pairs).
Learn a rule that predicts: from this current feature list, which direction nudges it toward the text features?
Slightly corrupt image features in random directions so the velocity field learns to steer reliably from many starting points.
Start with an image feature and take many small steps in the direction the velocity field says, reaching text features gradually.

paras: The paper changes how features adjust: from a single direct jump to a series of tiny nudges guided by a learned velocity field. The velocity field itself is the new trainable object — it learns the local direction to move at each moment of the transformation.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: alignment direction at each step
hidden.name: Velocity field accuracy
paras: A velocity field is a rule that assigns to each point in feature space a direction vector: nudge this way. The paper's hidden quantity is how well the learned velocity field predicts the correct nudge direction that moves image features toward their correct text features.

The paper measures this indirectly by training the velocity field on paired image-text features (with class coupling to preserve category labels) and checking that multi-step inference reaches the text features, unlike one-step methods. Higher accuracy means fewer misaligned classes after inference, because each step builds on the last one, so accumulated small nudges add up to reaching the target.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger influence on alignment. Highlights mark the velocity field's core components.

reads.html: The velocity field is like a set of trail markers: at every position in feature space, it points which way to walk next to reach the text features. Training teaches it to point correctly.

The velocity field satisfies flow matching: given a sample from the set of all image features and one from the set of all text features, it learns to move smoothly between them by predicting velocity, preserving which class each image belongs to via coupling strategy and noise augmentation.

paras: A one-step method tries to learn a direct mapping from image space to text space. When the two spaces are far apart and tangled (difficult dataset), this is like asking a neural network to learn a complicated function in one pass through the model. The network has to get every single direction right at once.

A velocity field approach is simpler: at each small moment in time, the field only needs to predict the next tiny nudge, based on where the image feature currently sits. Local adjustments are easier to learn than global transformations. By taking many steps, even small learned nudges accumulate, and the image feature drifts all the way to the text feature. The paper also uses two tricks to make this work: (1) coupling enforcement ensures that each image feature is paired with its correct text feature during training, so the velocity field learns to move class-by-class, not randomly, and (2) noise augmentation adds random perturbations to image features during training, so the velocity field learns to steer toward the target even when starting from slightly wrong positions, making it work reliably.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Start: image_x at position [10, 15]. Target text_z at position [90, 95]. Lambda = 0.3.
After one step with size 0.1: image_x moves to [10, 15] + 0.1 * [80.06, 79.97] = [18, 23.8].
At t=0.5, noise_offset = 0.3 * (1 - 1) * [random] = [0, 0]. Velocity purely aims at target.
Repeat for many steps: image_x keeps moving toward [90, 95] until overlap is achieved.

math.note: The equation shows that velocity combines the direct pull toward the text feature with random perturbations early on, then relies purely on direction as steps progress.

charts.title: One-step PEFT method
charts.note: One adjustment preserves easy classes but fails on difficult ones where features are far apart.

charts.title: Flow Matching Alignment (FMA)
charts.note: Multi-step alignment closes gaps gradually, maintaining easy classes and substantially improving difficult ones.

items.html: If the velocity field overfits to the few examples available, it learns to point toward memorized positions instead of a general direction. The noise augmentation helps by forcing it to steer toward the region, not exact points.

Taking 100 steps is slower than one-step inference. The paper uses early stopping: test different numbers of steps on validation data and pick the fastest that still aligns well. Beyond a certain point, more steps add no benefit.
Pairing each image to its correct text feature reduces training variety. If a class has only 2 examples, there are only 2 pairings. The noise augmentation creates synthetic variety to compensate.

items.b: Done right: velocity field + early stopping.
items.html: When the field is trained with coupling and noise, and inference uses only as many steps as needed, alignment succeeds even on difficult classes with few examples.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny few-shot setup: pick 2 or 3 classes from CIFAR or ImageNet, take 5-10 images per class, and use CLIP to extract features. Train the velocity field on the coupled, noise-augmented pairs. At inference, start with a test image feature, run it through the velocity field for different numbers of steps (5, 10, 20, 50), and measure how close it gets to the correct class's text feature. The demo must show that (1) more steps close the gap further, and (2) multi-step beats zero-step or one-step adjustment on the difficult classes.
demo.closing: The core claim: take enough small steps and even large gaps shrink. Fewer steps mean incomplete alignment on difficult data. One step leaves features stuck far away.
